Problem: For an open kinematic serial manipulator composed of multiple rigid links connected by motorized joints, each link can rotate or translate in 3D space. If we choose coordinate frames arbitrarily for each link, constructing the transformation from the base to the end-effector requires 6 parameters per link (3 translations + 3 Euler angles), leading to complex, non-standardized equations that must be recalculated from scratch for every robot design. Fix: The Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) convention solves this by imposing geometric constraints on frame placement: Every coordinate frame transformation between adjacent links is uniquely described by only 4 parameters instead of 6. The entire kinematic modeling process becomes systematic and programmable: software libraries (e.g., in ROS or MATLAB) can automatically construct forward kinematics and Jacobians directly from a simple numerical table. item.title: 06.Differential Kinematics & the Jacobian Pseudo-Inverse
item.description:
Divide each difficulty into as many parts as is feasible and necessary to resolve it. — René Descartes "اللهم إني أسألك فهم النبيين، وحفظ المرسلين، والملائكة المقربين، اللهم اجعل ألسنتنا عامرة بذكرك، وقلوبنا بخشيتك، إنك على كل شيء قدير" Map : Jacobian Review: The relationship between joint velocity and end-effector velocity. DH Parameters: How to describe the relationship between coordinate frames. Inverse Jacobian: How to derive joint velocities from the motion of the end-effector. Least Squares & Pseudoinverse: Solving equations when the number of joints differs from the number of constraints. SVD (Singular Value Decomposition): A more stable method for calculating the pseudoinverse. Robot Control: Using the inverse Jacobian within a control loop. The core idea : how to convert between end-effector velocities (what you want the robot's hand to do) and joint velocities (what the motors must actually do)The Big Picture: Why Differential Kinematics & ? In the previous lectures, we built the foundation of robot motion: 04.kinematics: Position Kinematics answered: "If my joints are at angles , where is my hand ?" (), and "To place my hand at , what joint angles do I need?" ().
05.Robot Coordinate Transformations & Differential Kinematics: We learned how to transform coordinate frames using Homogeneous Transformations () and introduced the Jacobian Matrix (), which relates small joint changes to small hand displacements: . The Engineering Problem of This note: In real life, robots do not "teleport" between positions. We don't just send target positions to the motors we control velocities in real time: Like saying : "Move the gripper smoothly to the right at ." To do that, the controller must answer Given desired hand velocity , what motor speeds must we command. Since , the obvious answer seems to be: But here is the catch: is almost never square (): Robots often have more joints than task dimensions (, redundancy) or fewer (). A non-square matrix has no regular inverse. Even when is square (), robots can hit singularities where , causing to blow up to infinity! Lecture 7 provides the full engineering solution: Using Least Squares Optimization, the Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse (), and SVD (Singular Value Decomposition) to invert the velocity relationship safely, and finally plugging it into a closed-loop PID controller.
The Jacobian Matrix Explained here is the linear bridge between Configuration Space (Joints) and Task Space (End-Effector).
Physical Interpretation of the Columns: Writing in terms of its columns: Column : The instantaneous velocity vector generated at the end-effector if joint moves at unit velocity () while all other joints remain frozen ( for ). Principle of Superposition: The total hand velocity is simply the weighted sum of the velocity contributions of each joint: Kinematic Singularities & Manipulability: Singularity: Any configuration where loses full rank (). Physical Meaning: Two or more columns of become collinear (linearly dependent). The robot loses the ability to move in that specific Cartesian direction, no matter how fast the motors spin! Manipulability Ellipsoid: If we feed the robot a unit sphere of joint velocities (), the Jacobian maps it into an ellipsoid of possible Cartesian velocities. Semi-axis lengths = singular values . Near a singularity, the ellipsoid collapses into a flat disk, indicating zero mobility along the collapsed axis. To compute the Jacobian of a complex 3D robot, we must first determine the position and orientation of every link. In 2D, simple trigonometry was sufficient. In 3D multi-joint arms, we use the standardized Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) Convention.
DH reduces the 6 DOF required to relate two arbitrary frames in 3D down to just 4 geometric parameters:بالبلدي كده: القاعدة الذهبية للـ DH حركتان على محور القديم: دوران بزاوية وإزاحة بمسافة . حركتان على محور الجديد: إزاحة بمسافة ودوران بزاوية . The DH transformation chain provides these vectors directly. Now we know that: This means given Joint Velocities, we calculate the End Effector Velocity. item.title: 05.Robot Coordinate Transformations & Differential Kinematics
item.description:
We see things not as they are, but as we are. Our perception is shaped by our previous experiences. — Dennis Kimbro "اللهم إني أسألك فهم النبيين، وحفظ المرسلين، والملائكة المقربين، اللهم اجعل ألسنتنا عامرة بذكرك، وقلوبنا بخشيتك، إنك على كل شيء قدير" The lecture started with 04.kinematics and then moved to something else. In this session part of our Robotics course We will start from fundamental concepts and work our way up to the Jacobian matrix, examining the equations that link these concepts to robot control and practical implementation. This lecture is crucial it marks the transition from simply understanding and calculating robot motion to being able to actively control a robot’s movement and speed. The lecture focuses on three main pillars:
Forward and Inverse Kinematics: How to calculate the position of the end effector, and how to determine the necessary joint configurations to reach a specific target location.(04.kinematics) we already learned this in the previous note. Coordinate System Transformations: How to calculate the position and orientation of any robot link relative to the global coordinate system using matrices. Differential Kinematics and the Jacobian: How to relate joint velocities to the motion and velocity of the end effector. We will begin by reviewing the basics, then delve into each of these topics in detail: Joint vector has one entry per joint. A revolute joint contributes an angle and a prismatic joint contributes a distance. All entries are called for convenience. A composite joint (e.g. a 2-axis wrist) is split into primitive 1-DOF joints, so a joint that rotates about 2 axes counts as 2 revolute joints.
The Grübler's formula Here for counting a mechanism's degrees of freedom. Task vector is the end effector pose (position plus orientation). in 3D (3 position + 3 orientation) and in 2D (). is the number of task coordinates the robot can actually control. A linear rail can't rotate, so its is smaller. A ground car can't fly, so for it (, , heading) and not 6. Redundancy and Degrees of Freedom it is possible to have a number of joints that exceeds the number of variables required in the task space. is . A robot with has extra freedom, and that matters for IK. For example: Consider a robot with 7 joints. Suppose you want to control 6 dimensions of the end effector. In this case, you have an additional degree of freedom we call it redundancy .In this example: What is the benefit of redundancy? A robot can reach the same location using different configurations, which provides flexibility in movement. For instance, a human can reach for a mobile phone with their elbow bent in various ways. This flexibility can be useful for: Avoiding obstacles. Staying within joint limits. Selecting a movement that consumes less energy. Maintaining a safe and appropriate configuration for the robot. Singular Configuration: it is a specific state of a robot in which its kinematic system loses some of its ability to move or be controlled in certain directions.the professor linked the concept of a "singularity" to the existence of an infinite number of solutions for the inverse mapping in certain cases.However, it is important to distinguish between these two concepts: The existence of infinite inverse kinematics (IK) solutions does not, by itself, mean that the robot is in a singular configuration. Mathematically, we address singularities by examining the Jacobian matrix specifically, when it loses its full rank. We will return to this point at the end of the Note ان شاء الله.In robotics, Coordinate System Transformations provide the mathematical tools to describe the position and orientation of objects or robot components across different reference frames, and to map coordinates between them Why do we need Coordinate Systems? تخيل عندك Robotic Arm فيه 3 Links. كل Link بيتحرك، وبالتالي كل Link ليه Coordinate Frame خاص بيه. يعني عندنا: World Coordinate System. Link 1 Coordinate System. Link 2 Coordinate System. Link 3 Coordinate System. السؤال: لو عرفت مكان نقطة بالنسبة للـ Link 3، أجيب مكانها بالنسبة للـ World إزاي؟ هنا بنستخدم Coordinate Let's distinguish between them World Frame and Local Frame: World Coordinate System: This is the primary, fixed Reference Frame relative to which we measure. We will denote it as Frame 0. Local Coordinate System: This is a Frame attached to a specific Link and moves with it. For example, Frame 1 is attached to the first Link, and Frame 2 is attached to the second Link. The Position of a point may differ depending on the Frame you are measuring relative to, even though the point itself hasn't changed.And This is completely normal if you think about it.Let's start with a 2D case like the example in the lecture. We have Frame 1 and Frame 2. Frame 2 could be: Rotated relative to Frame 1. Translated relative to Frame 1. Meaning we have Rotation and Translation.

First: Rotation Matrix: Explained Here ❣️❣️ Second: Translation Vector: Assume the Origin of Frame 2 has moved relative to Frame 1 by an amount: Meaning: it moved in the X direction, and in the Y direction. Now we have both Rotation and Translation.Instead of dealing with the Rotation Matrix alone and the Translation Vector alone, we combine them into a single Matrix. This is called the Homogeneous Transformation Matrix. Why do we do this? So we can represent Rotation and Translation in a single Matrix Multiplication operation. Notice that we added: A bottom row: . A last column containing the Translation. And we added an extra coordinate called the Homogeneous Coordinate. Instead of the point being: It becomes: Therefore: Meaning: We transform the Coordinates of the point from Frame 2 to Frame 1. Notice the order of the Subscripts here: The 2 is the Source Frame, and the 1 is the Destination Frame, according to the notation used in the notes.We have a point: , And a Transformation Matrix: We multiply: Result: Therefore, the point underwent: Rotation translation This is exactly the goal of the Homogeneous Transformation. Important note: When we multiply the matrix by the point in this form, we apply the transformation to the point written in Frame 2 to obtain its coordinates in Frame 1.Order of Matrix Multiplication Matrix Multiplication is not Commutative. Meaning: . You cannot change the order of the matrices. Also, when we use Column Vectors like in the lecture, the matrix on the right is executed first. When the robot has many links like you have Links: Then we multiply by the End Effector Coordinates to find its location in the World Frame. This is a very important idea in Robotics Software because you don't need to derive X, Y, and Z equations from scratch for every robot. You build a Transform for each Link, and then you compose the transformations. Example: , If I have a Point in Frame 2: Actual order: 1. : from Frame 2 to Frame 1. 2. : from Frame 1 to World Frame 0. Thus, we were able to go from Frame 2 to the World directly. In We describe the orientation using one angle . In , orientation needs three angles (Euler angles, also called roll X , pitch Y, yaw Z ), and the translation is a 3 Vector:Meaning with Column Vectors: Rotation around X. Then Rotation around Y. Then Rotation around Z. لكن خلي بالك: في Robotics فيه أكتر من Convention للـ Euler Angles؛ فلازم تعرف الـ Convention المستخدم في السؤال أو الـ Simulator Each matrix rotates about one axis, so the axis row and column are untouched (the "1" in the diagonal). looks odd, with its signs flipped relative to and . That's the right-hand rule: the cyclic order x→y→z→x flips the pattern for y. Order matters. , and different books/libraries use different conventions (e.g. XYZ vs ZYX), so check what your simulator or library uses. Multiplying them together () gives the full rotation matrix written directly in terms of the three angles:where the shorthand is , and likewise for and . So the nine entries are built only from the three angles , which is why 3 angles are enough to fix the orientation.Reading the angles back from (this ZYX convention, with = row , column ):Homogeneous Transformation in 3D: After calculating the Rotation Matrix in 3D, we can add Translation.Or in detail:This is the form you see often in Robotics and Computer Graphics. The Position is in the last column, and the Orientation is in the Rotation Matrix. Sensing the current pose: Joint encoders give , and FK gives the hand pose . Other sources can also give the pose: GPS works outdoors but has errors of several metres, so it's weak for small robots. Indoor Wi-Fi signal strength (RSSI): each position has a distinctive "fingerprint" of signal strengths from several access points (stronger near a router, weaker far away). A regression model maps the fingerprint to a position. Commanding the robot: In feedback control you compare the measured pose with the target pose to get an error in task space. The robot only accepts joint commands, so you must convert the target to joint angles. So FK is used to know where you are and IK is used to know what to command. المهم: الـ Kinematics بتساعدك تعرف العلاقة بين Joint Positions ومكان الـ End Effector So far, we have been dealing with Position and Orientation. But when we want to Control the robot, it's not enough to know where it is. We must also know: How fast is it moving? If we change a Joint Angle by a small amount, how much will the End Effector move? If we want the End Effector to move at a certain velocity, what velocities should we move the Joints at? Here comes the concept of Differential Kinematics: describes the relationship between joint velocities and the resulting linear and angular velocities of the end-effector.This linear velocity relationship is governed by a configuration dependent matrix called the **Jacobian Matrix:Let's return to the symbols: . This is the Forward Kinematics equation. Now we will start dealing with small changes. We have: . This is the small change in Joint Configuration. Example: ,And correspondingly: , This is the change in the Position of the End Effector. Meaning we want the relationship:This is called Forward Differential Kinematics: Is mapping from space of to the space of . The difference between Delta and Dot: (The professor focused on the difference between them.)The Dot means derivative with respect to time.Meaning if a Joint Angle changes with time, its derivative is its angular velocity.Assume you have a Function: . If we change by a small amount , then: . Using Taylor Series: If is small, , so the higher-order terms vanish:This is the idea we will use with Robot Kinematics. Generalizing the idea to Multi-variable Functions: In a robot, we don't have just one variable. We have:And the Position Vector:Each element in is a Function of all elements in . If a small change occurs in the Joints, the change in the first element of the Position will be: Notice that we used Partial Derivatives. Why? Because each Position Component depends on more than one Joint Variable. We repeat the same process for all Position elements.Converting equations to a Matrix: Instead of writing the equations one by one, we group them into a Matrix.Where is the Jacobian Matrix. Its general form: : Number of Joints. : Number of Task Space Variables we represent. Each element in the matrix is a Partial Derivative. Meaning: . This means The amount of effect of a change in Joint on Position Component . is , so it's often rectangular in general. : Number of Joints. : Number of Task Space Variables we represent. Then:Meaning: . Column is how the end effector moves per unit motion of joint . depends on the current , so it must be recomputed as the robot moves. The relation is a local linear approximation: it holds for small steps, not large moves. If Rectangular matrix and also non Singular,then it is is the true inverse. but if Determinant then it is singular so it is not true inverse. Otherwise means the pseudo-inverse . Depending on how we represent orientation and coordinate frames, there are three common formulations: Coordinate / Analytic Jacobian (): Obtained by taking direct partial derivatives of the forward kinematics vector function: . Simple and intuitive for 2D arms, but in 3D it uses Euler angle derivatives (), which can introduce artificial mathematical singularities (Gimbal Lock). Space / Geometric Jacobian (): Relates joint rates to the true physical spatial twist expressed in the fixed world frame. Built directly using the physical joint rotation/translation axes in 3D space without needing Euler angle derivatives. Body Jacobian (): Relates joint rates to the body twist expressed in the moving end-effector frame. Related to the Space Jacobian via the Adjoint transformation: . Both have the exact same rank and singular values. Position only (), from the notes. FK: , . Differentiate each output with respect to each joint: Column 2 only has an term because moves only the second link. Column 1 has both because moves the whole arm.Extension (singularity): . So the arm is singular at or , when it is fully stretched or fully folded. There the tip can't move along the arm's own direction, and blows up, which is the "infinite values" the lecturer describes. If you also include orientation , becomes with an extra row .This is Python, and it implements everything above for the 2-link arm. I ran it: the matrix-chain FK matches the closed form, the Jacobian matches finite differences to about , and the iterative IK converged to the target.import numpy as np def Rot(th): ## 2D homogeneous rotation c, s = np.cos(th), np.sin(th) return np.array([[c, -s, 0], [s, c, 0], [0, 0, 1]]) def Trans(a, b): ## 2D homogeneous translation T = np.eye(3) T[0, 2], T[1, 2] = a, b return T def fk(th1, th2, l1, l2): T01 = Rot(th1) ## frame1 -> frame0 T12 = Trans(l1, 0) @ Rot(th2) ## frame2 -> frame1: rotate, then shift l1 along x1 p2 = np.array([l2, 0, 1.0]) ## tip in frame 2 return (T01 @ T12 @ p2)[:2] ## tip in frame 0 (x, y) def jacobian(th1, th2, l1, l2): s1, c1 = np.sin(th1), np.cos(th1) s12, c12 = np.sin(th1 + th2), np.cos(th1 + th2) return np.array([[-l1*s1 - l2*s12, -l2*s12], [ l1*c1 + l2*c12, l2*c12]]) def ik_iterative(target, q, l1, l2, step=0.5, tol=1e-9, max_iter=200): """Repeat: small task-space step -> joint step via pseudo-inverse.""" for _ in range(max_iter): err = target - fk(*q, l1, l2) ## task-space error if np.linalg.norm(err) < tol: break dq = np.linalg.pinv(jacobian(*q, l1, l2)) @ (step * err) ## dq = J+ dp q = q + dq return q def ik_analytic(x, y, l1, l2): """Closed form: returns both elbow solutions, or [] if unreachable.""" c2 = (x*x + y*y - l1*l1 - l2*l2) / (2*l1*l2) if abs(c2) > 1: return [] sols = [] for th2 in (np.arccos(c2), -np.arccos(c2)): th1 = np.arctan2(y, x) - np.arctan2(l2*np.sin(th2), l1 + l2*np.cos(th2)) sols.append((th1, th2)) return sols l1, l2 = 1.0, 0.7 q = ik_iterative(np.array([1.1, 0.8]), np.array([0.3, 0.5]), l1, l2) print(q, fk(*q, l1, l2)) ## -> reaches (1.1, 0.8) How it maps to the theory: fk is the chain . ik_iterative is the differential relation applied repeatedly with small steps. This is the standard way IK is done on real robots, because the linear approximation only holds locally. The step factor keeps each move small. Near a singularity this loop becomes unstable, which is the problem the lecturer defers to next time.Pitfalls: Mixing up the direction of . Always check which frame the point starts in. Forgetting the homogeneous "1" in the point vector. Without it, translation is lost. Swapping the multiplication order of transformations. Entering clockwise angles as positive. Use the sign from the drawing. Assuming 3D orientations can be added like planar angles. Using for large motions. Take small steps and recompute each time. Trusting near or in the 2-link example. This is a focused review of the laws that appeared in the lecture.

item.title: 03.Robotics Controllers
item.description:
A man may fulfil the object of his existence by asking a question he cannot answer, and attempting a task he cannot achieve. — Oliver Holmes "اللهم إني أسألك فهم النبيين، وحفظ المرسلين، والملائكة المقربين، اللهم اجعل ألسنتنا عامرة بذكرك، وقلوبنا بخشيتك، إنك على كل شيء قدير" Learning goal Understand how a robot measures what it is doing, compares that measurement with a target, corrects its behavior with a controller, and how the robot's mechanical joints determine the motions it can perform. A robot needs two kinds of reasoning: Control: What should the motors do so the robot reaches the commanded position or speed? Mechanics: What motions are physically possible for the robot, and how many independent motions can we control? The control part connects a reference (the target) to a controller, a plant (the motor or robot), and usually a sensor that measures the result. The mechanical part describes the robot as links connected by joints, ending in an end effector such as a gripper or screwdriver. Think of the full loop this way: “I want this motion” calculate the error command the motors measure the actual motion correct the remaining error.~ What is a control system? A control system is a set of components that makes a system behave according to a desired objective. Reference:, the desired value, such as a target angle or speed. Plant: the physical system being controlled, such as a motor, robot joint, or complete robot. Controller: calculates a control action from the error. Actuator: turns the control command into physical action. A motor driver and motor are common examples. Sensor: measures the actual output, such as position or speed. Output:, the actual measured or produced result. Error:, the difference between what is desired and what is measured. In the lecture, the motor's PWM duty cycle, , is an example of a control command. The controller changes to affect the motor's speed.
![](https://techietory.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/rbt_51.png) Analog for better understand Suppose you apply a fixed PWM duty cycle to a motor. If the load becomes heavier, the motor may slow down. In open loop, the controller does not notice the speed change, so it continues sending the same command. In closed loop, a speed sensor detects that the motor is slower than the reference. The controller increases the command to reduce the error. For unity feedback, the error is is the reference. is the output measurement. is the error sent to the controller. Three useful cases:
If , the measured output is below the reference. If , the measured output is above the reference. If , the reference and measured output are equal at that instant. For the motor example, a positive error may cause the controller to increase PWM duty cycle , a negative error may cause it to decrease PWM duty cycle . The exact action depends on how the plant and controller are defined, but the objective is to drive the error toward zero. The output is subtracted from the reference at the summing point: . This is called negative feedback. It does not mean that the system's output must be negative, it describes the sign used when feeding the measured output back into the comparison. useful analog تخيّل إنك سايق عربية وعايز سرعتك تبقى 100 كم/ساعة. بتقارن السرعة اللي إنت عايزها بالسرعة اللي العداد بيقيسها. لو العداد بيقول 80، فيه فرق موجب فتزوّد البنزين. لو بيقول 110، الفرق يبقى سالب فتقلّل البنزين. دي فكرة الـ feedback: القرار بيتغير بناءً على النتيجة الفعلية، مش على الأمر الأصلي بس. A properly designed feedback loop can improve: Accuracy: it corrects deviations between the reference and output. Disturbance rejection: it can compensate for changes in load or plant parameters. Time response: it can make the output respond more effectively to a command. Stability: with suitable controller design, feedback can stabilize a plant that is unstable on its own. These benefits are not automatic. Feedback can also amplify sensor noise or cause oscillation if the controller is badly tuned.Why can open-loop accuracy drift? Motor resistance, magnetic strength, friction, load, and other physical properties can change with time or operating conditions. A fixed command-to-output calibration (معايرة) may then become inaccurate. An Open-loop system may need recalibration. Closed-loop control measures the result and attempts to compensate for these changes automatically.What does an encoder measure? An encoder converts motion into a signal that a controller can read. الـ Encoder هو حساس (Sensor) بيحوّل الحركة الميكانيكية، مثل دوران عمود الموتور، إلى بيانات رقمية (Digital Data) يقدر الكمبيوتر أو الـ Microcontroller يفهمها optical disc encoder: which measures angular position. If position is sampled repeatedly, it can also be used to estimate speed. تخيّل إن عندك موتور بيلف، وإنت محتاج تعرف زاوية دورانه. بدل ما تقيس الزاوية بشكل مستمر، الـ Encoder بيقسّم الدورة إلى عدد من المواضع، وكل موضع بيكون له كود رقمي. An optical disc contains tracks divided into dark and bright sectors.
Each track is read by an optical sensor, often described as a photocoupler consisting of a light source (such as an LED=~) and a light-sensitive receiver (~={gray}such as a phototransistor).=~
A bright/reflective or transparent region allows the receiver to detect light. A dark/opaque region blocks or reduces the light. The sensor converts this difference into a digital bit, usually treated as or . The bits from the tracks form a code for the current angular sector. الـ Track هو مسار دائري على قرص الـ Encoder، وبيساهم في تحديد الموضع باستخدام قيمة ثنائية (Binary Value). We are not animals. We are not a product of what has happened to us in our past. We have the power of choice. Stephen Covey "اللهم إني أسألك فهم النبيين، وحفظ المرسلين، والملائكة المقربين، اللهم اجعل ألسنتنا عامرة بذكرك، وقلوبنا بخشيتك، إنك على كل شيء قدير" Kinematics = the geometry of motion, ignoring what causes it like power or torque It ignores forces, torques, and accelerations. Only position and velocity exist in this world. Anything about "will the battery handle this?", "how much torque does the motor need?", or energy belongs to dynamics, a different course topic. افترض إن عندك ذراع روبوت طوله مترين. في الـ Kinematics، تقدر تحسب مكان إيده لما تغيّر زوايا المفاصل، حتى لو مش عارف نوع الموتور المستخدم. لكن في الـ Dynamics، لما تطلب منه يشيل حمولة وزنها (5,kg)، محتاج تدرس العزوم والكتل والقصور الذاتي عشان تعرف هل الموتور يقدر ينفذ الحركة المطلوبة. It splits into two parts: Position kinematics: It relates joint angles and positions to the location and orientation of the robot's end effector. This is the core part we will be working on today.(This lecture) Differential (velocity) kinematics: This examines the relationship between joint velocities and the velocity of the robot's end-effector, often utilizing the Jacobian. This is an extension of the current lecture the detailed derivation is not covered here. (Next lecture) Why ignore forces? A robot arm is a chain of rigid links. Where its hand ends up depends only on the shape of the chain (link lengths and joint angles), not on how hard the motors pushed. So geometry alone answers "where is the hand?". For every formula you get three layers: The equation — boxed, using the same symbols as the lecture. A term table — what each symbol is and what job it does inside the system. A folded How we reached it callout — the full derivation, step by step, written as > [!example]- so it stays collapsed until you click it. Click the arrow beside any folded callout to audit the algebra line by line. Nothing is hidden to trick you — folding only keeps the visible layer clean for revision. The entire lecture is built around one loop: a reference (what you want) flows through a controller and a plant (motor, joint, robot), a sensor measures the result, and the measurement is subtracted from the reference to form the error. The controller's only job is to process that error and drive the actuator — here the PWM duty cycle — so the error shrinks toward zero. Every equation later in this note is just a mathematical refinement of this single idea.Sign logic (what the error tells the controller to do): Negative feedback means the output is subtracted at the summing point (). It does not mean the output value itself is negative — it only names the sign convention of the comparison. Why feedback is worth the hardware: accuracy (corrects drift), disturbance rejection (compensates load changes), better time response, and it can stabilize a plant that is unstable on its own. Open-loop drift happens because resistance, friction, and magnet strength change with time, so a fixed calibration goes stale — closed-loop re-measures and compensates automatically. Unity feedback assumption assumes the sensor chain has gain exactly , so the measurement can be compared directly with the reference. Every formula in Parts 3–5 inherits this assumption. The encoder is the sensor of the loop: it converts mechanical rotation into a digital code a microcontroller can read. Its math answers four questions: how many codes exist, how fine is one step, what angle does a code mean, and how do we get speed out of position samples.How we reached it: Each track gives one binary digit: or . With independent tracks, a reading is an -bit word, and the number of distinct binary words on bits is: Check with : the words are → codes, matching the lecture. How we reached it: worked example with 3 tracks With tracks: And with only tracks: , so — exactly the two cases the lecture compares. What this formula does not tell you here is the idealized sector position, not the exact true angle inside the sector — the true angle can be anywhere within the -wide sector. That gap is precisely the quantization error: the difference between the real continuous angle and the angle represented by the digital code. Worst case, the true angle sits anywhere in a -wide sector, so the uncertainty is bounded by the resolution ( if each code is read as its sector's centre). How we reached it: gearbox shrinking one encoder step With , the motor turns revolutions while the output shaft turns . So one motor-side encoder step of appears at the output as: Practical meaning: mounting the encoder on the motor side of a large reduction gives an effective resolution far finer than the raw — the gear ratio divides the step size, not just the speed. How we reached it: from to a finite difference Start from the definition of angular velocity as the derivative of angle: A microcontroller cannot measure an infinitesimal . Over a small but finite interval , approximate: Substituting gives the backward finite difference: It is literally "distance in angle ÷ time taken" — the slope of the angle samples. Accuracy degrades if is too large or the speed changes a lot within one interval. Gray code caveat Real encoders usually encode sectors in Gray code, where neighboring sectors differ in exactly one bit — so a boundary read can never produce a wildly wrong multi-bit error. The goal shifts from measuring the motor's angle to controlling it. But remember — real delays and mechanical limits can still change the picture. Integral action erases steady-state error, but its accumulated history makes it slow to react to sudden changes. Derivative action adds anticipation: it looks at how fast the error is changing and resists rapid motion, acting as a damper.The D-term's built-in weakness Derivatives amplify high-frequency noise: a tiny but fast jitter in the sensor reading produces a large , so a noisy measurement can shake the actuator. That is why production controllers filter the derivative path. Tuning philosophy The goal is to balance the three effects — never to maximize any single gain. There is no universal triple — the right values depend on the plant, its behavior, and its limits. The three routes: simulation (model + disturbances, test many combos), manual tuning (adjust on the real system, carefully), and automatic tuning (algorithms pick gains from the measured response). Whichever route, you watch these specs:Implementation PID can live in analog hardware (op-amp circuits) or software — in a microcontroller it is simply the same arithmetic repeated every sampling period, which is exactly what Part 7 formalizes. A microcontroller cannot integrate or differentiate continuously — it samples the system every seconds and approximates both operations with arithmetic on samples. Let be the error at sample . Read the current sensor measurement . Get the reference . Compute . Add the current error to the integral accumulator. Compute the difference . Combine P + I + D into the raw command. Clamp the result to the actuator's valid range. Save the current error for the next cycle. Send the bounded command to the motor driver. float Kp = 1.0f, Ki = 0.1f, Kd = 0.05f; float integral = 0.0f, previousError = 0.0f; const float Ts = 0.01f; // 10 ms sampling period const float uMin = 0.0f; // minimum PWM duty cycle const float uMax = 1.0f; // maximum PWM duty cycle float pid(float reference, float measured) { float error = reference - measured; // step 3 integral += error * Ts; // step 4 (software integrator) float derivative = (error - previousError) / Ts; // step 5 float u = Kp * error + Ki * integral + Kd * derivative; // step 6 if (u > uMax) u = uMax; // step 7 (clamping) if (u < uMin) u = uMin; previousError = error; // step 8 return u; // step 9 } // Call pid() at a fixed rate (every 10 ms), with fresh encoder data. Assumptions & production caveats The code assumes it is called at a fixed rate — if the real interval varies, the integral and derivative must use the actual elapsed time. Production controllers also add derivative filtering and proper anti-windup logic (so the accumulator does not keep growing while the actuator is saturated). Control tells the robot how to move; structure decides which movements are possible at all. The math here counts independent variables.Definition Degrees of freedom (DOF) = the number of independent variables needed to describe the motion or configuration of a system. For a joint that variable is an angle or a displacement ; for a free end effector it is position plus orientation. A prismatic displacement is measured relative to a chosen reference position, and can be positive or negative depending on the coordinate direction. = number of independent motions needed to specify the end effector's pose (position + orientation). = number of independent joint variables, collected in the joint vector:The two numbers are different quantities: is required to be able to do the task at all. → redundancy: the same end-effector pose is reachable by multiple joint configurations — useful for obstacle avoidance or comfortable poses, but it depends on the robot's geometry and the task. Grübler's formula estimates a mechanism's mobility — its total number of independent motions — from its parts. The logic: count the motion every free link would have, then subtract what the joints lock away.How we reached it: the formula itself from constraint counting Free motion before constraints. With links ( of them ground), the moving links each have free motions: Motion removed by each joint. In a -dimensional space, two connected links have possible relative motions, but a joint of freedom permits only of them — so joint removes relative motions. Over all joints: Subtract: Exactly the lecture's intuition: possible motion before constraints − motion blocked by joints = mobility. Example 1: planar three-joint open-chain arm A planar arm with three revolute joints: (planar world) — three moving links plus the ground , each revolute joint , so Substitute: Meaning: three independent motions — so with one motor per joint, three motors fully control the arm. Example 2: planar four-bar linkage Both ends connected to the ground: , (three moving links + ground), , each → Substitute: Meaning: one degree of freedom. Move the input link and every other part must follow deterministically — so one motor drives the whole mechanism. Adding a second uncoordinated motor would force two incompatible motions into the same constrained loop → internal stress or jamming. Sketch the mechanism and mark the fixed ground/base. Count all links including the ground → . Count every joint → (a 2-DOF joint is still one joint, with ). Decide planar () or spatial (). Add the joint freedoms → . Substitute into Grübler's formula. Sanity-check the result against the actual geometry and loops. 00.RoboticsFundamentals
item.description:
One of the advantages of being disorderly is that one is constantly making exciting discoveries. A. A. Milne "اللهم إني أسألك فهم النبيين، وحفظ المرسلين، والملائكة المقربين، اللهم اجعل ألسنتنا عامرة بذكرك، وقلوبنا بخشيتك، إنك على كل شيء قدير" Drawing embed actionsDrawing previewOver all map: SENSOR ↓ Physical world ↓ ADC ↓ Raw value ↓ Calibration ↓ Physical quantity ↓ Control System ↓ Decision/Correction ↓ Actuator ↓ Physical world ↓ SENSOR ↺ A robot is modeled the same way you'd model any living organism, and that's explicitly the design inspiration: living things sense their envidronment, process that information with a "brain," and act. A robot has four core components: Sensors = "sense" (temperature, touch, camera/vision, humidity, etc.) Sensors is a transducer (محوّل طاقة): it converts non-electrical energy into electrical energy. Actuators(المشغلات) = named from "act" (motors, etc.) they take an action, i.e., they do something physically. An actuator does the opposite job: it converts electrical energy into motion. The main example here is the DC motor: current in a magnetic field produces force/torque.Important idea: The robot “understands” only electrical/digital signals. The physical world is analog and continuous, so there must be conversion between the world and the computer. The program counter, PC, holds the address of the next instruction. Cycle: Fetch: Use PC to get the next instruction from memory. Decode: Control unit interprets the instruction. Execute: Arithmetic/logic unit performs the operation: load/store, add, jump, etc. Then PC is updated to the next instruction. Practical meaning for robotics:Your robot program is not “thinking continuously” in a magical way; it is repeatedly executing instructions very fast. Real-time behavior comes from running this loop fast and predictably enough.That is why robot programs are often written as an infinite loop:state = initial_state() # start with "zero experience" while robot_is_on(): z = read_sensors() # 1) SENSE take input state = update(state, z) # 2) PROCESS update internal state a = choose_action(state, objective) # decide the (optimal) action execute(a) # 3) ACT drive the motors This is the classic sense–process–decide–act loop. SENSOR ↓ Physical world ↓ ADC ↓ Raw value ↓ Calibration ↓ Physical quantity ↓ Control System ↓ Decision/Correction ↓ Actuator ↓ Physical world ↓ SENSOR ↺ used during execution (working memory, holds current:state/data) sensor readings, current state, intermediate calculations, variables, stack/heap. Two classic types: Built from flip-flop-like circuits, often around 6 transistors per bit. Fast. Keeps data while power is on. Expensive and lower density. Used for cache and small fast buffers. Stores bits as charge in capacitors. Much denser/cheaper per bit. Leaks charge, so it needs periodic refresh. Used for main memory. Cache memory is usually SRAM: small, very fast memory placed between processor and main RAM to reduce the speed mismatch.Historically it evolved through generations, each solving the previous one's hardness: ROM (mask ROM): Written once at the factory. Cheapest, oldest, cannot be reprogrammed at all. PROM (Programmable ROM): You can write it yourself, but only once after that it's fixed, like ROM. EPROM (Erasable PROM): Can be fully erased and rewritten, but requires special hardware (historically UV light). EEPROM (Electrically Erasable PROM): Erased using an electrical signal instead of UV(الأشعة فوق البنفسجية) much more convenient. This is the basis of modern Flash memory (e.g., SSDs, and the flash memory in a microcontroller that holds your robot's program). In embedded robots: The robot program is commonly stored in flash/ROM-like memory, copied or executed from there, and RAM is used for runtime variables. -+-+ Microprocessor: Just the CPU core alone on its own board. You need to add memory, I/O interfaces, etc. separately (e.g., Raspberry Pi's main chip). Microcontroller: A complete system-on-a-board processor + memory + I/O interfaces bundled together (e.g., Arduino). Simpler to program because everything you need is already wired together; you just read/write pins. The I/O interface exists because the processor/memory operate at very high speed while inputs/outputs are comparatively slow the interface buffers/manages that speed mismatch (e.g., buffering fast output data so the slower output device can consume it at its own pace). Fetch: The Program Counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. The processor goes to that memory address and pulls the instruction into an Instruction Register, then increments the PC. Decode: The instruction (in machine code) gets decoded broken down into micro-instructions telling exactly what operation to do (e.g., "load this register," "add these two values"). Execute: The decoded micro-instructions actually run. Most processors used in robotics are RISC architecture. What is RISC? RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) is a central processing unit (CPU) design philosophy that uses a small, highly optimized set of simple instructions instead of a large collection of specialized commands
RISC Source note LEC2 from micro controllers course lecture 2. To keep this fast without waiting on slow DRAM every cycle, a small amount of fast SRAM cache sits between the processor and main memory.A sensor's job is to convert one form of energy into the electrical energy the robot's processor can understand: Example: a microphone converts mechanical (sound wave) energy into electrical signal.filtersNow its ADC TurnAnalog Digital Real-world sensor output is analog (continuous), but the processor only understands digital data. So an A/D converter (ADC) is required it samples the analog signal at discrete points to produce digital data. الـ ADC بيحوّل الإشارة الكهربائية اللي جاية من Sensor إلى رقم. ال Raw value → الرقم الخام، مش بالضرورة له معنى فيزيائي مباشر. ف ال Calibration → نعرف الرقم ده بيمثل كام فيزيائيًا. ال Inverse calibration → نحول القيمة الفيزيائية المطلوبة إلى command يفهمه الـ hardware. ال Control system → يقيس النتيجة ويصحح الأمر باستمرار. أهم فكرة: ال Calibration = ربط عالم الـ hardware الرقمي بالعالم الحقيقي الفيزيائي. ![](https://skl-sklc-tinymce-2021.s3.amazonaws.com/comp/2021/02/mceclip4_1613046954.gif)You have a coil of wire (with a battery attached via brushes) sitting inside a magnetic field created by a permanent magnet (North/South poles). Current flows through the coil.Where current, magnetic field, and motion meet, a force appears (the "current–field–motion" law Fleming's left-hand rule). Its magnitude:
sin 90° = 1 → force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to B. In the coil, = +90° on one side and −90° on the other (currents flow in opposite directions relative to B). In a coil, the current on one side flows "up" and on the other side flows "down" so the two sides of the loop experience equal and opposite forces ( and ), but applied at two different points (separated by the coil's width). Equal-and-opposite forces applied at different points produce a torque عزم (turning effect), not a net linear force (which would just cause balance/cancellation if applied at the same point).Since (the loop's area): Key takeaway: Since , , and are fixed by the motor's construction, torque is directly controllable through current torque is proportional to current: where = torque constant (a property of the specific motor a "strong" motor has high , a "weak" one has low ).Units check: is in (force × distance, i.e., like Joules but for rotation), is in Amps, so: Torque only appears when there's resistance to motion a constraint. If a robot arm is moving freely with zero resistance (no friction, no air), torque = 0 for that motion; but the moment it hits a wall or you grip the moving part with your hand, kinetic energy converts into torque, current increases (since ), and heat increases () which is why gripping a stalled motor makes the wire heat up and can burn it out. Practically: you care about torque wherever there's a physical constraint (e.g., a robot pushing a pen down onto paper needs a small torque to press against the surface, while simultaneously moving in the perpendicular direction motion and torque can happen simultaneously in orthogonal directions).Rewriting Torque with Angular Velocity the Motor's Two Core EquationsAngle of rotation is measured in radians (dimensionless). Dividing angle by time gives angular velocity: For an ideal motor (100% energy conversion, no losses), electrical power in equals mechanical power out: Electrical power doesn't care about the Direction. but Mechanical power does. Setting them equal: Substituting :So we get the two fundamental "ideal DC motor" equations: The second equation is the motor's back-EMF: a spinning motor generates a voltage proportional to its speed, using the same constant as the torque equation (a beautiful symmetry from energy conservation).A real motor isn't lossless it has coil resistance and coil inductance . Model the real motor as an ideal motor in series with a resistor and inductor :Since (the back-EMF), applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law:Rearranging in terms of : since ,For many practical motors, inductance is negligible compared to resistance (), so the term drops out, leaving the steady-state approximation:This shows an inverse relationship between torque and speed for a fixed applied voltage : if torque goes up, speed must go down (and vice versa), since (battery voltage) is fixed.Rearranging to isolate :This is a straight line (linear relationship) when you plot (y-axis) vs. (x-axis) for a fixed voltage . Two convenient points define it: Stall torque (at , i.e., motor not moving max current, max torque): No-load (max) speed (at , i.e., nothing resisting the motor it spins as fast as it can): This torque-speed line/curve is a standard way motors are characterized: low speed high available torque; high speed torque drops to (near) zero.A real motor's datasheet gives you three key electrical parameters: torque constant coil resistance coil inductance Plus: minimum/maximum rated voltage (exceeding max voltage excessive current overheating burnt coil). Practical implication: if you increase applied voltage , the whole torque-speed line shifts up (higher stall torque, higher max speed) but you're bounded by the motor's rated maximum voltage; exceed it and the resulting current/torque will overheat and destroy the coil.This gives you the full chain: what a robot is made of how it thinks in a loop how sensors turn physics into numbers the four lenses (kinematics/dynamics/statics/control) for studying motion and the concrete physics/math of the DC motor that actually produces that motion.

item.description: I am always doing that which I can not do, in order that I may learn how to do it. — Pablo Picasso Dua "اللهم إني أسألك فهم النبيين، وحفظ المرسلين، والملائكة المقربين، اللهم اجعل ألسنتنا عامرة بذكرك، وقلوبنا بخشيتك، إنك على كل شيء قدير" Overview The course focuses on motion, plus one AI topic. The source of motion — covered in this lecture. From simple to complex mechanisms. Everything is built from links and joints Simple Machines Big mechanical systems = combinations of simple machines: The Lever — Egyptians lifting stones: F₁ × d₁ = F₂ × d₂ The Pulley — rope over a wheel Motion Transmission — rotary ↔ linear conversion A car is an assembly of many such simple mechanisms + motion transmission elements. Deriving equations of motion (position, velocity, acceleration) ignoring forces.Why Ignore Forces? High-level tasks are specified in position and velocity, not energy. "I want to arrive fast" — fuel consumption is not the object of study here. Motion with forces — Newton's Second Law: F = m·aEnergy View At constant velocity on a perfectly smooth road, no force is needed → ideally zero power. Real consumption comes from air resistance and friction — remove both and consumption is zero. Torque is "force's brother": it appears when motion is resisted. Quantum Scale At quantum scales Newton's second law fails (position and momentum cannot both be exactly determined). Advanced robot design may use quantum dynamics (Schrödinger's equation) with generalized formulations. Conceptual note only. Equilibrium of forces for stationary structures. We want robots to choose the right action within their experience — like humans. Simulators ROS (Robot Operating System) — the standard framework Webots — a 3D simulator where you design a robot and program it (C or Python) Lab robots (e.g., a small humanoid on a Raspberry Pi, programmed in Python) Simultaneous Localization and Mapping SLAM = Simultaneous Localization and Mapping Connection to RL This is exactly the state / action / transition structure used in Reinforcement Learning. Summary Robotics combines mechanics, mathematics, and AI — from simple levers to intelligent autonomous agents.
